issues.legal_issue: A validating statute that applies to previously acquired undertakings can retrospectively validate earlier acquisition actions that complied with the earlier enactment and are not inconsistent with the validating statute.
material_facts: The undertaking was taken over under an earlier enactment that was later held invalid.
The later enactment incorporated the acquisition scheme, applied expressly to undertakings already taken over, and included a clause validating prior orders, notifications, proceedings, and acts.
The challenged acquisition notification was issued in the manner contemplated by the earlier enactment and was not shown to conflict with the later enactment.
issues.conclusion: The later enactment operated retrospectively, and its validation clause deemed the earlier acquisition notification valid under the later enactment.
issues.legal_principle: The enactment's definitions and provisions applying to undertakings already taken over showed that its material and operative provisions were retrospective. The validation clause covered prior actions that would have been properly taken under the earlier enactment if it had been valid, subject to consistency with the later enactment. The absence of the usual words deeming prior notifications to have been issued under the new enactment did not alter that effect.

predicates.acquisition_validation_proceeding: The proceeding challenges the validity of an acquisition action taken before a later enactment that addresses prior acquisitions.
predicates.later_law_covers_prior_acquisitions: The legislature enacted a law whose operative scheme applies to undertakings already taken over.
predicates.prior_action_would_have_been_proper_unde: The acquiring authority took the earlier action in the manner the earlier enactment required, assuming that enactment had been valid.
predicates.prior_action_does_not_conflict_with_late: The earlier acquisition action is not inconsistent with the provisions of the later enactment.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges a prior acquisition covered by a later law, an action that would have been proper under the earlier law and does not conflict with the later law is treated as valid under the later law.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature with authority over the subject may retrospectively validate actions taken under an enactment that was void, including because it contravened fundamental rights.
material_facts: The earlier acquisition enactment had been held void for lack of legislative competence.
The legislature later enacted a law on the subject and included provisions intended to validate actions taken under the earlier enactment.
The challenge argued that retrospective validation could not cure action taken under a law that violated fundamental rights.
issues.conclusion: The legislature was competent to enact a retrospective law validating actions taken under a void enactment, including an enactment void for contravening fundamental rights.
issues.legal_principle: A legislative power to enact laws on a subject includes the power to enact them retrospectively, subject to constitutional limitations. The Court distinguished the question of automatic revival considered in Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh, which did not decide whether a legislature could retrospectively validate actions taken under a void law. It relied on the principle that a legislature may validate executive actions through legislation ancillary to its subject-matter powers, discussed in United Provinces v. Mst. Atiqabegum and Piare Dusadh v. The King Emperor, and on the general retrospective-legislation principles in Union of India v. Madan Gopal Kabra, M.P.V. Sundararamier & Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, M/s. J.K. Jute Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Mt. Jadao Bahuji v. Municipal Committee, Khandwa, Jadab Singh v. Himanchal Pradesh Administration, and Raghubar Dayal Jai Prakash v. Union of India. The Court held that invalidity for lack of legislative competence and invalidity for contravention of fundamental rights both render the enactment void, and that the asserted limitation on retrospective validation had no basis.

rule.if: retrospective_validation_proceeding and legislature_has_subject_matter_authority and later_validating_law_is_retrospective and prior_action_was_taken_under_void_law

predicates.retrospective_validation_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a legislature's attempt to validate earlier executive action through a later law.
predicates.legislature_has_subject_matter_authority: The legislature has authority to enact laws on the subject addressed by the later law.
predicates.later_validating_law_is_retrospective: The legislature enacted a law that operates retrospectively to validate earlier action.
predicates.prior_action_was_taken_under_void_law: An authority took the challenged action under an earlier enactment that was void.

issues.definition: A legislature with authority over the subject can retrospectively validate earlier action taken under a void enactment.

issues.legal_issue: A retrospective law validating a property acquisition can satisfy the requirement that a person be deprived of property only by authority of law.
material_facts: The property was taken under an earlier enactment that was void.
A later enactment applied retrospectively and purported to validate the acquisition action.

The constitutional property guarantee required deprivation to be by authority of law, while the separate protection against retrospective criminal punishment expressly referred to a law in force at the time.
issues.conclusion: The retrospective operation of the later enactment supplied authority of law for the acquisition and satisfied the property guarantee.
issues.legal_principle: The property guarantee required deprivation by authority of law but did not use the phrase “law in force at the time.” By contrast, the protection against retrospective criminal punishment used that phrase, indicating that retrospective operation was excluded there. Accordingly, a subsequent law operating retrospectively could validate the acquisition for purposes of the property guarantee.

predicates.property_deprivation_proceeding: The proceeding challenges a deprivation of property on the ground that it lacked legal authority.
predicates.later_law_operates_retrospectively: The legislature enacted a law that applies to events occurring before its enactment.
predicates.later_law_validates_the_acquisition: The later law purports to validate the earlier acquisition action.

issues.definition: A retrospective law that validates an acquisition supplies authority of law for the property deprivation.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory compensation scheme is not shown to violate the constitutional requirement of just equivalent compensation merely because it does not expressly use market value, when the challenger supplies no adequate evidence that each available basis fails to provide a just equivalent.
material_facts: The acquisition law provided three alternative bases for calculating compensation and allowed the licensee to choose the basis.
The bases included a multiple of average net annual profits, a share-value calculation, and a calculation based on asset values with specified additions.

The challenger asserted that the compensation was inadequate and alleged a market value for the undertaking, but supplied no satisfactory supporting material showing how that value was determined or demonstrating that compensation under each basis failed to provide a just equivalent.
The undertaking was a going commercial concern, and the Court considered that its value could not necessarily be assessed mainly by reference to its buildings or machinery.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the compensation scheme was rejected because the challenger had not supplied sufficient material to establish that compensation under every available basis failed to provide a just equivalent.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 31(2) as it stood before the Fourth Amendment, the principles for determining compensation had to ensure a just equivalent of the property acquired. State of West Bengal v. Mrs. Bala Banerjee permitted scrutiny of whether the statutory principles accounted for the property's true value. But the legislature's failure to refer expressly to market value was not conclusive or presumptive proof of inadequacy; the Court had to assess what each basis would provide, and a challenger had to place satisfactory and sufficient material before the Court to show that each basis failed to provide a just equivalent. The availability of alternative bases and the licensee's choice among them were also relevant.

rule.if: compensation_scheme_challenge and compensation_law_offers_alternative_bases and owner_can_choose_basis and challenger_lacks_sufficient_evidence_that_each_basis_is_inadequate

predicates.compensation_scheme_challenge: The proceeding challenges whether a statutory acquisition compensation scheme provides a just equivalent for the property acquired.
predicates.compensation_law_offers_alternative_base: The legislature provided more than one basis for calculating compensation for the acquired property.
predicates.owner_can_choose_basis: The owner or licensee may choose which available compensation basis will be applied.
predicates.challenger_lacks_sufficient_evidence_tha: The challenger did not provide satisfactory evidence showing that compensation under every available basis would fail to provide a just equivalent.

issues.definition: A challenge to a compensation scheme is not established when the scheme offers bases the owner may choose among and the challenger does not sufficiently show that every basis is inadequate.
